title: The Bell of Cold Spring
premise: Late-night radio host Paloma Nakamura begins receiving calls from listeners who died the week before, each asking her to 'give back what was taken.' She dismisses it as a cruel hoax until she finds her childhood imaginary friend, Tomás, waiting on her porch, unchanged since 1989, and realizes he is the voice behind the calls. Tomás pulls her into the history of Cold Spring, where in 1974 the town drowned a girl named Esperanza and stole the mission bell that anchored the town's uneasy peace, and every descendant who profited from the theft has been dying in order of complicity. Paloma must decide whether to expose the town's founding crime on air, betraying her own family's role, or stay silent and let the deaths continue; she broadcasts the truth, returns the bell to the dry riverbed where Esperanza died, and the calls stop — but the final caller, in a voice she recognizes as her own, tells her the bell only borrows its keepers, and now it has her.
about_author: Isandro Reyes is the pen name of a former small-town news reporter who spent a decade covering municipal archives and unsolved disappearances along the California coast. He writes horror rooted in civic secrets, believing every town keeps a bell it refuses to ring.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. During her overnight show 'The Cold Spring Line,' a caller named Ruth describes her own funeral from last Tuesday, then the line fills with the dead. Paloma assumes a prank, but the calls match obituaries exactly. Emotional beat: professional skepticism curdling into private dread as she cuts to music and sits shaking in the booth.

chapters.title: The Boy on the Porch
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She finds Tomás, her imaginary friend from childhood, waiting on her porch, forty years older in her memory but unchanged in the flesh. He speaks only in the callers' phrases: 'give back what was taken in 1974.' Emotional beat: the vertigo of a skeptic confronting the one impossible thing she once loved.

chapters.title: What the Archive Won't Say
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, intercut with 1974 fragments from Esperanza's diary. In the county archive, Paloma finds a gap: a missing page, a redacted inquest, a photo of the mission bell being lowered into the riverbed. Emotional beat: the slow horror of realizing her town's history is a constructed silence.

chapters.title: The Order of Complicity
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. He explains the rule: the dead call in the order the town wronged them, and the living die in the order their families profited. Paloma maps the deaths against the 1974 inquest signatories — and her grandfather's signature is fourth from the top. Emotional beat: loyalty and truth beginning their war inside her.

chapters.title: Grandfather's House
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She confronts her dying grandfather, who confesses the town drowned Esperanza Vidal after she accused the founding families, then melted down nothing — the bell itself was buried in the riverbed to 'keep the peace.' Emotional beat: grief for a man she loved, and fury that his love was built on her silence.

chapters.title: Static in the Family Line
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The third family on the list dies publicly, and the town turns on Paloma, accusing her of a hoax that 'spooked' a heart attack victim. Her station manager, a descendant on the list, suspends her. Tomás begins to fade at dawn. Emotional beat: isolation, and the temptation to simply stop digging.

chapters.title: The Dry Riverbed
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV with Tomás. They dig at the riverbed at night and uncover the bell, uncorroded, cold as well water, engraved with every name the town took. When she touches it she hears Esperanza's final hour. Emotional beat: awe and terror fused — the bell is not evidence, it is a witness that wants to testify.

chapters.title: Second on the List
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The second family dies; her grandfather is now next, and the town's remaining founders offer her a deal: silence, money, her grandfather's life. Tomás warns that the bell doesn't bargain. Emotional beat: the corrupting offer of power — protection purchased with complicity.

chapters.title: Open Line
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, climax. She takes back the airwaves, puts her grandfather on as a caller, and lets him confess to the town live, naming every family, then leads a procession to the riverbed and raises the bell. It rings once by itself. The dead stop calling. Emotional beat: cathartic, terrifying justice outside every law.

chapters.title: The Keeper
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, resolution. Her grandfather dies peacefully, forgiven. Tomás says goodbye, finally aging. The show ends — until a new caller, in Paloma's own voice, says the bell only borrows its keepers. She looks at her hands, cold as well water. Emotional beat: quiet, ambiguous dread — justice won, and a debt inherited.
